lines.text: VUGA NDAKUMVA
UNDERSTANDING SLEEP
AND MENTAL WELLBEING
Mental Health Educational Content Library | Expanded Chapter 08
Purpose. To help readers understand sleep physiology, recognize common sleep problems, develop
supportive routines, and know when professional medical or psychological care is needed.
Audience. General adult readers, older adolescents with appropriate support, caregivers, educators,
and community health educators.
Publication status. Evidence-informed educational draft. This handbook is not a diagnostic tool or a
substitute for individualized professional care. Clinical review, Rwanda-specific referral checks,
accessibility review, and human-reviewed translation are required before public release.
Edition 1.0 | 11 November 2026 | English
Important: If you are extremely sleepy, avoid driving or operating machinery. If you have severe
difficulty breathing during sleep, sudden loss of consciousness, or other acute symptoms, seek
appropriate medical care.

Learning goals and chapter map
After this chapter, a learner should be able to describe the main stages and regulators of sleep,
recognize common patterns of sleep difficulty, explain the relationship between sleep and emotional
wellbeing, identify supportive daily habits, and seek appropriate professional assessment when
needed.
Section What readers will learn
1-4 Why sleep matters; circadian rhythms; sleep pressure; NREM and REM sleep
5-9 Sleep needs; inadequate sleep; insomnia and other disorders; mental health connections
10-14 Practical sleep habits; contextual barriers; treatment, medications and safety
15-19 Case studies, guided exercises, assessments, answers, glossary and references
1. What is sleep, and why do we need it?
Sleep is a natural, recurring state in which the brain and body undergo coordinated changes. It is not
simply a period of inactivity. During sleep, the brain cycles through different stages that support
attention, learning, memory, emotional processing and physical functioning. The value of sleep is not
measured by duration alone: timing, continuity and how rested a person feels during the day also
matter. [1-3]
A single difficult night is common and does not necessarily indicate a disorder. Sleep becomes a
greater concern when problems persist, are distressing, or interfere with safe and effective daily life. A
person with adequate time in bed may still get poor-quality sleep because of repeated awakenings or
an underlying disorder.
Why the topic belongs in mental health education
Sleep and mental health affect each other. Stress, anxiety, depression, trauma-related symptoms and
other difficulties may interfere with sleep. Repeated poor sleep can also worsen concentration,
irritability, emotional regulation and coping capacity. This does not mean that every person who sleeps
poorly has a mental illness. [3,4]
2. The body clock: circadian rhythm
The circadian rhythm is an approximately 24-hour timing system that influences when we feel alert,
sleepy, hungry and ready for activity. Light, daily activity and regular waking patterns help synchronize
it. The brain receives information about environmental light and uses it to coordinate the sleep-wake
cycle. The hormone melatonin typically rises as darkness approaches, helping signal nighttime. [2]
For example, a student who stays awake on a phone until very late and sleeps until noon on weekends
may find it difficult to become sleepy at an earlier school-night bedtime. However, teenagers naturally
tend toward later sleep timing than younger children; this biological shift should not be mistaken for

Sleep pressure
A second process is the drive to sleep that builds while we are awake. Sleep pressure generally
increases as waking hours pass and decreases during sleep. Together, sleep pressure and the
circadian rhythm influence when we fall asleep and wake up. Caffeine can temporarily reduce our
sense of sleepiness but does not replace the restorative functions of sleep. [2]
3. What happens during the night?
Typical sleep contains both non-rapid-eye-movement (NREM) and rapid-eye-movement (REM) stages,
cycling several times. Patterns change with age and across the night. [5]
Stage Broad description
NREM 1 A light transition from wakefulness into sleep; easy to awaken.
NREM 2 More established sleep; body functions slow and external awareness decreases.
NREM 3 Deep or slow-wave sleep; especially prominent earlier in the night.
REM Brain activity changes; vivid dreams are common and memory/emotional functions are
supported.
No single stage is the only "important" stage. Normal sleep includes a balance across stages, and
consumer sleep trackers cannot reliably diagnose a sleep disorder based solely on their stage
estimates.
4. How much sleep is generally recommended?
Recommended sleep amounts depend on age, and they describe population guidance rather than a
rigid score for each individual. Some people need more sleep when ill or recovering from lost sleep.
Age group Typical recommended sleep
6-12 years 9-12 hours per 24 hours
13-17 years 8-10 hours per 24 hours
18-60 years At least 7 hours, commonly 7-9 hours
61-64 years 7-9 hours
65 years and over 7-8 hours

young child may have limited control over sleep time. Educational advice must acknowledge these real

5. What is insufficient or poor-quality sleep?
Insufficient sleep means obtaining less sleep than the body needs. Sleep deficiency can also involve
poor timing, interrupted sleep, or a condition that reduces restorative sleep. Possible daytime
consequences include low alertness, difficulty remembering information, slower reaction time, changes
in mood and greater risk during driving or hazardous tasks. [3]
Common signs worth noticing
• Frequently feeling sleepy or unintentionally dozing during the day.
• Struggling to concentrate at school, work or during conversations.
• Needing much more time than usual to complete simple tasks.
• Becoming more irritable or emotionally reactive after poor nights.
• Feeling unrefreshed despite giving yourself adequate opportunity to sleep.
Symptoms can also arise from anemia, medication side effects, other illnesses, depression or other
conditions. A professional assessment can help determine the cause.
6. Insomnia: more than one bad night
Insomnia involves difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or returning to sleep after waking, despite an
adequate opportunity to sleep, with associated distress or daytime impairment. Temporary insomnia
may follow stress, illness, travel, grief or major changes. Chronic insomnia is a more persistent clinical
pattern and should not be diagnosed from a simple website checklist. [7-9]
Common maintaining patterns
A person who worries about whether they will sleep may become increasingly alert at bedtime.
Spending extra hours awake in bed, monitoring the clock, or irregular sleep timing can sometimes
maintain the problem. Persistent insomnia may also coexist with pain, anxiety, depression, substance
use or other sleep disorders.
Example: A university student spends several nights awake before examinations. After the
examination ends, the student keeps worrying about sleep and begins staying in bed much
longer to "catch up." The difficulty continues. A clinician can assess whether insomnia-focused
treatment is appropriate.
7. Other sleep conditions people should know about
Obstructive sleep apnea
Sleep apnea may involve repeated breathing interruptions, loud snoring, gasping or choking during
sleep, and daytime sleepiness. Not everyone with sleep apnea snores. People with these symptoms
should seek medical assessment; sleep hygiene alone cannot treat the underlying breathing disorder.

Circadian rhythm sleep-wake difficulties
Some people cannot align their natural sleep timing with work, school or social schedules. Shift work,
jet lag and delayed sleep timing may contribute. Treatment depends on the pattern and may require
specialist guidance.
Restless legs, parasomnias and hypersomnolence
Uncomfortable sensations that improve with moving the legs, unusual behaviors during sleep, or
severe daytime sleepiness deserve evaluation. Falling asleep unexpectedly or experiencing sleep
attacks should not be assumed to result only from a busy schedule.
8. How sleep and mental health interact
Stress and worry
When the body is on alert, it can be harder to settle at night. Sleep loss can make daily stressors feel
harder to manage. Gentle routines may help, but people facing ongoing insecurity or hardship also
need practical support.
Anxiety
Worry about future events or sleep itself may prolong wakefulness. Persistent sleep difficulties and
anxiety symptoms should be assessed together rather than treated as unrelated issues.
Depression
Depression may be associated with difficulty sleeping, early waking or sleeping much longer than
usual. Changes in sleep alone do not establish depression, and treatment decisions require careful
assessment.
Trauma-related symptoms
Nightmares, hypervigilance or a feeling of unsafety may disrupt rest. Survivors should not be
pressured to close their eyes, disclose memories, or perform relaxation exercises that increase
distress.
Bipolar disorder
A markedly reduced need for sleep accompanied by unusually high energy, elevated or irritable mood,
racing thoughts or impulsive behavior can be a warning sign that needs prompt professional
assessment. This is different from ordinary insomnia accompanied by fatigue.
9. Everyday habits that can support sleep
Healthy sleep routines are useful for general wellbeing and can complement clinical care. They are not,
on their own, an adequate treatment for chronic insomnia disorder. [1,8-10]
• Choose a wake-up time that is as consistent as your responsibilities allow.
• Seek natural daylight and appropriate activity during the day.
VUGA NDAKUMVA | Mental Health Content Library | Educational draft 5
• Build a predictable winding-down routine: reading, quiet conversation, gentle music or another
calming activity.
• Reduce bright screen use close to bedtime if feasible, especially when it keeps you alert.
• Limit caffeine in the afternoon and evening if it affects you.
• Keep the sleep space as dark, quiet, comfortable and safe as reasonably possible.
• Avoid using alcohol as a sleep aid: it can fragment sleep and has other risks.
• If an environment is unsafe or crowded, focus on feasible improvements and seek practical support
rather than blaming yourself.
10. Practical barriers in Rwanda-relevant daily life
A reader may share one room with family members, work evening shifts, study under difficult
conditions, manage caregiving duties or have limited privacy. Advice should prioritize realistic actions.
For example, a household may coordinate a quieter period, reduce unnecessary night lighting, or plan
a more reliable morning routine when possible. These are illustrative situations, not claims about all
Rwandan households.
When poverty, housing insecurity, severe stress, violence or illness disrupt sleep, an individual routine
cannot resolve the underlying problem. Health education should connect people to medical, social and
practical support where appropriate.
11. Evidence-based care for persistent insomnia
What is CBT-I?
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured treatment that addresses
sleep-related patterns of thinking and behavior. It can include education, tailored behavioral
strategies, cognitive approaches and follow-up. Multiple clinical guidelines recommend
multicomponent CBT-I as first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults. [8,9]
Specialist CBT-I may include methods such as sleep restriction or sleep compression. These should not
be copied from a handout without assessment, especially for people with certain medical or psychiatric
conditions, excessive daytime sleepiness, high-risk work, or complex sleep problems.
Medication and supplements
A clinician may consider medication depending on symptoms, age, other conditions, pregnancy status,
interactions and treatment history. Sleeping pills can have side effects and may not address the
underlying cause. Do not start, combine, stop or change prescribed medicines on the basis of this
chapter. Melatonin is not a universal cure for insomnia and suitability varies. [7,10]
VUGA NDAKUMVA | Mental Health Content Library | Educational draft 6
12. When should someone seek professional help?
Consider an appointment with a qualified healthcare professional when sleep difficulty persists,
significantly affects mood, concentration, study or work, or occurs alongside loud snoring, breathing
interruptions, repeated nightmares, unusual movements, severe daytime sleepiness, chronic pain or
symptoms of a mental health condition.
Urgent medical assessment is warranted if a person has severe or unusual breathing problems,
episodes of losing consciousness, serious injury associated with sleepiness, or new concerning
symptoms. If a person is dangerously sleepy, they should not drive or operate machinery. If there are
thoughts of suicide or immediate danger, seek urgent emergency assistance through available local
emergency services or the nearest emergency department.
Where symptoms suggest mania or a significantly reduced need for sleep with marked behavioral
changes, seek prompt clinical assessment.
13. Four everyday learning scenarios
Case 1 - Examination week
A secondary-school learner studies very late, uses a bright phone in bed and struggles to wake for
class. The learner feels irritable and forgetful.
Reflection: What realistic changes to study timing and evening routine might help? How might teachers
or caregivers support the learner?
Case 2 - Shift work
A healthcare worker rotates between late and early shifts and becomes sleepy during travel. Family
responsibilities limit recovery time.
Reflection: Which barriers require schedule or workplace support? Why is drowsy travel a safety
concern?
Case 3 - Persistent worry
An adult worries about falling asleep and checks the clock throughout the night. Sleep problems
continue for weeks and affect work.
Reflection: What makes this different from a single sleepless night? Why might CBT-I assessment help?
Case 4 - Nighttime breathing concerns
A family notices that one adult snores loudly, sometimes gasps during sleep and remains very tired
during the day.
Reflection: Why should this person seek medical assessment rather than only trying herbal tea or an
earlier bedtime?

14. Guided activity A - My seven-day sleep
observation
For seven days, readers may record sleep patterns without trying to force a target. This exercise is for
awareness, not diagnosis or clinical sleep restriction. Avoid recording sensitive details on devices that
are shared or monitored.
Day Approx. bedtime / wake time Restfulness and daytime notes
After the week, consider whether patterns change with shift work, phone use, stress, noise, illness,
caffeine or caregiving. Bring the notes to a clinician if a sleep problem is ongoing. If recording sleep
increases anxiety, stop tracking.
15. Guided activity B - A gentle evening routine
Choose one or two realistic steps, not a rigid checklist: (1) identify tomorrow's priority tasks earlier in
the evening, (2) choose a quiet activity for the final part of the day, (3) adjust brightness or noise
where feasible, and (4) allow yourself to rest without checking the clock repeatedly.
Reflection: Which step is feasible in your home? What barrier would require someone else's
cooperation? A routine should be adapted to safety, disability, caregiving and work schedules.
16. Guided activity C - Distinguishing a worry from a
plan
Write down an ordinary concern earlier in the evening if doing so feels comfortable. Divide it into
"something I can act on tomorrow" and "something I cannot solve tonight." Choose one practical next
action for tomorrow. Do not use this exercise to dismiss real danger, pain or urgent needs.
Example: "I may be late for work" can become "I will prepare my bag and check my transport
plan." If a concern involves an unsafe environment or a serious medical symptom, practical
safety assistance takes priority over relaxation.

lines.text: 17. Knowledge assessment
1. Does the need for sleep change across ages?
2. Is sleep quality relevant even when total hours seem adequate?
3. What two major processes influence sleep timing?
4. Does every difficult night indicate insomnia disorder?
5. Why can late caffeine use be relevant?
6. Is sleep hygiene alone the recommended treatment for chronic insomnia?
7. What symptoms suggest possible sleep apnea?
8. Should someone copy sleep restriction instructions from an article?
9. Can emotional distress and poor sleep affect each other?
10. What should a dangerously sleepy driver do?
18. Assessment answers and explanations
1. Yes. Children and teens usually need more sleep than adults.
2. Yes. Fragmented or mistimed sleep can still impair functioning.
3. Sleep pressure and circadian rhythm.
4. No. Isolated sleep difficulty is common.
5. It can interfere with the ability to feel sleepy or fall asleep.
6. No. Multicomponent CBT-I is recommended as first-line treatment for many adults.
7. Snoring, observed breathing pauses or gasping, and excessive daytime sleepiness.
8. No. Such treatment should be tailored and supervised.
9. Yes, the relationship may be bidirectional.
10. Avoid driving and seek appropriate help.
19. Glossary
Circadian rhythm: An approximately 24-hour cycle regulating alertness and many bodily functions.
Sleep pressure: The biological tendency to become sleepier with time awake.
REM: A sleep phase associated with characteristic eye movements and often vivid dreams.
NREM: Non-rapid-eye-movement sleep, including lighter and deeper stages.
VUGA NDAKUMVA | Mental Health Content Library | Educational draft 9
Insomnia: Difficulty sleeping despite an opportunity to sleep, causing distress or impairment.
CBT-I: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia, a structured evidence-based treatment.
Sleep apnea: A sleep-related breathing disorder that requires medical assessment.
Sleep hygiene: Daily routines and environmental practices that can support healthy sleep.
